An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). This figure is consistent with existing predictions from the Standard Model, which forecast an value of 1.497 picoseconds for this parameter. Furthermore, an updated limit of 3.2 picoseconds was placed on $R_{\text{eff}}$, the ratio of decay rates for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ and $B^0\rightarrow K^+K^-$, which is also influenced by quark interaction forces and was found to be 6.4 times the probability of $B^0_s$ over $B^0$ production, with an uncertainty of 2.5 times the present precision. This led to the reconfirmation of the stability of the $R_{\text{eff}}$ ratio in the particle physics community. In addition, cross-section data for the process $p\bar p\rightarrow B^0_s\bar B^0$ was obtained with a rate of 47.8 nanobarns or 47 times the predicted value based on the total $p\bar p$ cross-section at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV and production probabilities for $B^0_{s}\bar B^0$ and $B^0\bar B^0_s$ pairs that were found to be 11.3 ± 1.2 nanobarns, 3.08 ± 0.33 nanobarns, and 0.38 ± 0.18 nanobarns, respectively. Finally, upper limits on rates for decay processes $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ (excited states) and $B^0_s\rightarrow D^+D^-$ were established at the level of 0.8 and 0.5 nanobarns, or 0.3 and 0.2 times the predicted values based on quark combination

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. A notable finding emerges, suggesting that the solution to this control problem can be equivalently formulated as a continuous-time version of the Generalised Maximum Likelihood estimator, which serves as a theoretical foundation for an efficient numerical solution algorithm. A type of numerical method, which combines finite element discretisation of the spatial component and a time step containing multiple sub-intervals for the temporal component, is proven to be computationally stable. Moreover, it can be demonstrated that this method yields a consistent and asymptotically stable solution when the time step decreases. This research was initially presented at the 16th conference on applied mathematics held in Pitlochry, Scotland. The data and research underlying this paper are available in various mathematical repositories. A key contribution of this research is the convergence proof of the numerical solution algorithm, which represents the continuous-time GMLE estimator. This validation is particularly important because it addresses an unfilled gap in the research on numerical solutions to stochastic control problems. The efficiency of the proposed numerical method is further highlighted by demonstrating that the condition requiring the time step to be sufficiently small can be satisfied using multiple sub-intervals, which facilitates the use of higher-order finite element methods. The value of this research is enhanced by the inclusion of an illustrative example, alongside the theoretical proof, to demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed numerical solution algorithm. The associated code is accessible in the most commonly used mathematical programming languages. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, our observations underscore the need for a comprehensive explanation of cosmic ray anisotropies across the entire energy spectrum. Given the limited understanding of high-energy cosmic sources and magnetic field dynamics, we highlight the anisotropy of the most energetic cosmic rays as a potential window into extreme relativistic magnetohydrodynamic processes, likely inherent in the extragalactic environment itself. Our study reinforces the significance of in-depth anisotropy analysis in the energy domains controlled by extragalactic cosmic rays. Ultimately, the discovery of anisotropies in the most energetic cosmic rays encourages a comprehensive re-examination of established perspectives on their origins. Our research outcomes are applicable to next-generation, larger cosmic ray detection facilities. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Additionally, an analysis of data revealed slight differences with results obtained from the LHC's other experiment, CMS, particularly in collisions that are not very central and for particles with lower momenta than 2 GeV/c, although the reasons for these distinctions are yet to be determined and require further investigation. In summary, this study marks a significant breakthrough in researching heavy-ion collisions and provides a framework for continuing this type of research with future experiments, such as the LHC's ALICE and CMS experiments and the NASA's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider's STAR and PHENIX experiments with increased sensitivity. In the future, such research will enable better understanding of the quark--gluon plasma's initial conditions and the effectiveness of quantum chromodynamics in this domain. In the current study, the effective temperature of the quark--gluon plasma's viscosity was found to be approximately 0.084 along with an initial temperature of the quark--gluon plasma's temperature field that was described by a Gaussian distribution, with a standard deviation of 1.98 times the mean and a mean of 0.529 times the central barrel's saturation density. In addition, the research found that the average path length of the quark--gluon plasma's initial state was approximately 5.2 times the central barrel's saturation density and the density of the quark--gluon plasma's initial state

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we showcase the applicability of our theory to practical scenarios through concrete examples. Notably, our research demonstrates the benefits of handling inconsistencies explicitly, thereby bypassing the need for underlying data management systems to make implicit inferences about missing values. This is particularly significant when utilizing external data sources, where little to no information is available about the underlying data generation principles. In such cases, our approach provides a robust and versatile framework that leverages the native support for nulls and implications present in modern database management systems, allowing for more efficient handling of queries and ensuring consistency with the existing data, without compromising on data generality. This research has implications for pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging, which we propose should be considered as special cases of query validation. This is achieved by modifying the underlying relation database with techniques like tuple deletion and insertion, thereby ensuring consistency with the underlying implications and providing a viable solution for incorporating external data sources. This is particularly evident when examining scenarios like merging peer-to-peer networks and managing open data on the web. Finally, this research has implications for Four-valued logic and data merging, which it incorporates into the framework, but is not the primary focus of study. This is because the underlying logic is seen as a means to an end, rather than an end in itself, with the underlying purpose being to provide a robust framework for handling inconsistencies that can be further applied to various data management tasks, including but not limited to data merging, where four-valued logic is inherently supported by the underlying system. This research was initially presented at THRA'21.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. These empirical examples demonstrate the TV-PARX model's ability to forecast target variables with higher precision compared to conventional SARMA models. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for the time-varying specification of dynamic models, encompasses the results of previous research on paralogous models, and offers empirical and forecasting performance evidence. Ultimately, the TV-PARX model offers a significant contribution to the field of time-series forecasting, particularly for count-based data sets undergoing dynamic changes. In its current form, however, the model requires a large sample size. As a result, we recommend it particularly for large-scale datasets, such as those found in electronic health records. In these cases, the TV-PARX model is a particularly useful tool, capable of modeling complex dynamics and forecasting target variables with greater precision than existing methods. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Notably, our analysis indicates that the relation often approximated as $|z_c|\approx 1.445 R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ leads to universality class values of $\gamma$ that vary significantly from the expected values, differing from these expected values by more than the associated systematic and statistical uncertainties for all relevant scenarios. Nonetheless, the reliability of our findings is demonstrated by the consistency with the already existing more precise determination of $\gamma$ for $N=4$. Nonetheless, the relevance of these findings to $N=1$ and $N=3$ cases remains uncertain due to the limited available data. Our results are essentially a verification of the earlier obtained, more precise determination of $\gamma$ for $N=4$ despite the associated uncertainty being greater than that of the previously mentioned calculation. Nonetheless, for $N=2$ we have obtained a new estimate of $\gamma$ along with the associated universal edge singularity characteristics. Finally, our analysis suggests that the approximation often used to determine $\gamma$ from $|z_c|$ may be less accurate than previously thought, with the associated uncertainty being significant, especially for the relevant universality classes in two and three dimensions. Consequently, our study recommends direct determination of $\gamma$ from the fit of renormalized fields instead of approximation via the edge singularity exponent $z_c$. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality can be used to extend the results from [10, 20] to the "hard but noiseless" case, where the average Hamming weight in the discrete curve is finite. We also investigated the properties of the optimization landscape relative to the Hamming cost function and obtained insights into its structure. Finally, our analysis provided a threshold value that marks the boundary between a region where the Hamming weight becomes trapped at 0 and one where the weight can drop below 1 when the AMP algorithm is applied. We also analyzed this threshold in relation to the "information ratio" in the "hard but noiseless" scenario. We intend for our inequality to be highly versatile, given the numerous unanswered questions it raises regarding the properties of the TAP free energy and the AMP algorithm in the context of Z2 synchronization and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. We also believe our inequality can be useful in other applications, such as random constraint satisfaction problems and gauge theory. We have made our code public for ease of use by others. We trust that our work will encourage further research on the topics mentioned above. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We further developed a new analytical approach to model the fractal scintillation patterns caused by the detectors' photon statistics, which are essential for accurate calibration of the system. We successfully tested these developments using simulated and real data, achieving a precision of 0.01 for the aerosol depth at an angle of 45 degrees, and we believe this precision could be achieved within the precision of the aerosol depth measurement itself. Therefore, the precision of the measurement is primarily determined by the system's accuracy rather than the technique itself, and we expect this precision to hold true for any similar wide-field optical array that includes CCD detectors at the focus of a telescope. We also present a straightforward method to calculate the systematic error of the vertical aerosol depth measurement, which is given by the square root of the number of pixels, and we estimate that increasing the detector from 1 to 4 kilopixels would increase the systematic error from 0.012 to 0.020. We emphasize that the precision of 0.01 can be achieved with a small array if it is positioned at the focus of a telescope, which provides natural illumination and precise calibration. We highlight the potential of this technique to be used in a variety of settings, such as from a mobile platform in atmospheric science, to a fixed location in astrophysics, with the potential to integrate a large array in a plane parallel to the detector, which would allow for the measurement of the aerosol depth with a precision of 0.005 within a hour. We propose a possible future detector with a precision of 0.01 and discuss the potential of using time and space encoding to further improve the precision to 0.005. We have made the software and data from this study available for other researchers to use

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed code is now publicly available on the GitHub site www.github.com/XiaoningRan/ObjectPoseCode. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. It
facilitates entry point interfaces for Python and offers integration with
scipy.sparse data structures. Furthermore, GGLasso provides an intuitive, user
friendly interface through the graphical user interface provided by Pycairo. This
framework encompasses a wide range of applications, from neuroimaging to
genomics, and offers various optimization solver options, including the use of
a block-wise Newton method and a gradient descent alternative, along with
other features. The package builds on the original lasso implementation by
Newton, (2011) and includes extensive documentation on usage, mathematics, and
publication references. The package is designed to be easily extensible, allowing
the integration of new algorithms and models with ease. The framework itself
is highly modular, with distinct components for model specification, optimization, and
post-processing results, making it easily modifiable and customizable for
specific purposes. The package is successfully put to use in the exploration
of a certain brain glucose transmission network. The Graphical Lasso scheme
is comprised of multiple challenging optimizations that present difficulties
in initialization, slow convergence, and the need for scalable solutions.

extensible framework. The purpose of GGLasso is threefold: firstly, it presents
a concise yet comprehensive description of the underlying mathematical framework;

of diverse Graphical Lasso subcases; thirdly, it offers the implementation of

By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. Overall, this method shows significant potential for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations. Through the utilization of the expansion up to the second-order term, the study's findings held true, indicating that higher-order expansions are unlikely to lead to better performance. Additionally, the research highlighted the limited impact of the method's accuracy in sampling fast molecular degrees of freedom, emphasizing the need for enhanced numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations, despite the widespread adoption of damped oscillatory integrators. Nevertheless, the study emphasizes that the performance of these integrators is solely determined by the resolution of the fast degrees of freedom, which is primarily influenced by the time step, rather than the numerical method itself. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness and simplicity of our approach by applying it to real-world data, including a case study of scientific collaboration networks. Additionally, our results show that our approach is comparable to other multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that incorporate inter-layer connections, even in large-scale networks. Our approach and associated code are available online for further use and modification. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. By introducing the Dirac operator in the conformally flat 
de Sitter spacetime, we derive the explicit solutions for the wave function, which can 
be compared to previously obtained results using other approaches. We also analyze the 
energy spectrum of the massive fermion in the de Sitter spacetime. For the case of 
negative energy, the solutions are associated with the conformal factor $\xi^2 = r^2$ 
and the energy levels are given by $E = -\hbar c r_0^{-1}$, where $r_0$ is a constant 
determined by the boundary conditions. We also examine the energy levels for positive 
energy, which are identified as the multiplicity of the massive conformal fermion. 
Additionally, we determine the minimum energy threshold to be $\hbar c r_0^{-1}$, 
above which the massive conformal fermion can exist within the de Sitter spacetime. 
Notably, this energy threshold corresponds to the mass value $m r_0 = \hbar c^{-1}$. 
We also find the relationship between the energy levels and the angular momentum in 
the de Sitter spacetime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the wave functions of the 
Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime form closed shells, which are connected 
to the concept of quanta in quantum mechanics. We then explore the possibility

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our data and analyses also indicate that the common water-entry phenomenon of partial-seal is often misclassified under the surface-seal regime. Furthermore, our research reveals that the widely accepted 93 ft/s (28 m/s) water-entry speed threshold, indicating a transition from surface-seal to partial-seal, is too broad and needs revision. Ultimately, our studies aim to contribute to the design of underwater equipment, ensuring that parts of such devices do not become waterlogged due to improper water-entry procedures. Our results specifically provide a basis for predicting the surface-seal regime's behavior in depth ranges relevant to underwater technology applications. Our experimental approach involves observing the water-entry interactions of spheres at various velocities, ranging from 10 to 110 ft/s (3 to 33 m/s), and depths of 1 to 30 ft (0.3 to 9 m), using high-speed video capture technology. Although our primary focus is on single-sphere water-entry interactions, we have also observed the water-entry behaviors of pairs of spheres traveling at the same velocity, both moving directly towards each other and moving in opposite directions. Our research reveals the complex dynamics of water-entry interactions, featuring the formation of cavities, water-entrapment phenomena, and surface-seal regimes, among others. Our findings aim to enhance our understanding of these interactions, thereby facilitating the development of more efficient and properly designed underwater equipment. Our experimental approach can be applied to studying similar water-entry interactions involving other geometric shapes. Our data are publicly available for use in verifying numerical models and other related research objectives. Our study includes an analysis of the relationships between velocity, depth, geometry, and water

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. The analysis of an individual $\theta$-term's components, which are composed of a Kaluza-Klein monopole, a Kaluza-Klein invariant density of topological origin, and a density of topological origin that is invariant with respect to the global symmetries, reveals that the range of the effective theory is an arbitrarily small section of the moduli space's boundary, near which the low-energy approximation holds. We also examined a particular case where a pair of $\theta$-terms and a pair of charged scalar fields are present. In this scenario, the effective potential's minimum, which defines the range of the effective theory, is composed of a Kaluza-Klein monopole's self-dual part, while the effective theory's symmetry is generated by the $O(4)$ rotational group of the moduli space. The rotation of this effective theory's symmetry group from the $O(4)$ to the $SO(4)$ type, which corresponds to the inclusion of the Kaluza-Klein monopole's anti-self-dual part, results in the effective theory's symmetry being global rather than gauge. We found that this rotation is linked with the Kaluza-Klein monopole's anti-self-dual part's inclusion and with the emergence of the Witten effect. Moreover, we established that this effect, along with the range of the effective theory, is indefinitely large and forms a Bragg-like spectrum along the moduli space's boundary near which the low-energy approximation holds. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Furthermore, we find that cubanite's unique orbital behavior is driven by the specific arrangement of its atoms and crystal fields, offering insights into the underlying physics and potential pathways for adjusting the orbital selectivity through, for example, applying pressure or substituting atoms. Moreover, our analysis indicates that cubanite's molecular structure allows for an indirect interaction between adjacent iron ions, explaining the observed ferromagnetic coupling, and we propose that such an indirect interaction could be a critical factor in achieving ferromagnetism within transition metal compounds. Moreover, we determine the cubanite band structure and identify possible states for extracting information on the electron interaction and potential phases of the material. Lastly, our work highlights the cubanite as a versatile compound that can be modified to exhibit a variety of electronic properties while maintaining its unique features. Our methods and findings are also applicable to other compounds sharing cubanite's crystallographic and chemical characteristics.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. This breakthrough poses an significant improvement upon previous records of up to ten phonons emitted in one second, achieving a remarkable ten-fold increase while using the same quantum device. This groundbreaking achievement is published in Science at 124, 1061 (2021) and was featured in an cover story by the journal. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface. We also discuss its possible electronic phase transitions and propose that it could be an suitable platform for exotic exotic quantum phases, such as topological quantum phases driven by spin-orbit coupling. We think this model is particularly interesting if it can be combined with a raster scan microscope, as this setup would allow for the direct correlation between the local symmetry and the resulting electronic band structure, providing a unique understanding of the exotic quantum phases that this model is capable of exhibiting. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Additionally, we outline the approach for generating these states in laboratory settings using catalytic devices, and examine the potential applications of SPCCSs in optical systems. Finally, we discuss the theoretical limitations of success probability and catalytic gain for both beam splitters and parametric amplifiers, as well as the relationship between their associated parameters. Moreover, we establish the relationship between the number of photons required for state detection and the catalytic parameters, and present the approach for modifying these states to mitigate the restriction associated with detecting single photons at the input ports. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to determine the coordinates and spinor indices of the points where the null surfaces intersect, allowing us to determine the physical properties of the electromagnetic field from its components of the Weyl tensor. Additionally, we outline the procedure for obtaining the complex conjugate of the Weyl tensor, which is essential for determining the complex conjugate of the electromagnetic field. Moreover, we illustrate this method by applying it to the Kerr solution, ultimately leading to a detailed understanding of the rotational black hole's electromagnetic field properties. Ultimately, this review demotes its complexity to a level suitable for advanced undergraduate students studying General Relativity.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, the proposed framework has been applied to an real-world problem involving the creation of drug compounds, achieving results that are equivalent to the current state of the art methods. The proposed method has been made available for public use through the NEOS Server of optimization, where users can access it along with guidance on its usage. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Furthermore, our detailed dataset guidelines may contribute to the creation of similar datasets for other abdominal organs, as it is open-source and accessible at this link https://esophagus.cvresearch.org/. Our future plans involve experimenting with other networks, batch normalization, and data augmentation techniques to improve our model's performance. Our findings highlight the potential of a streamlined clinical approach that relies solely on CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with acceptable precision. To facilitate this goal, we developed the Dilated Dense Attention Unet, a fully automated model that successfully segmented esophageal tumors from a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with diverse anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By incorporating multilingual code-switching, we advocate for the development of more inclusive NLP systems that reflect the true nature of language usage among multilingual individuals. This will, in turn, facilitate a smoother integration of NLP technologies into their daily lives. To achieve this goal, we emphasize the importance of a framework that enables easy integration of multiple language models, potentially leading to a unified model that can handle multiple languages with high performance. By overcoming the barriers of language isolation, we can unlock the potential of NLP to benefit multilingual communities even further. To achieve this, we propose a simple, modular architecture that combines the strengths of different language models, thereby providing a feasible and scalable solution. This research is part of an ongoing project to develop an open-source, multi-language NLP platform that can be easily extended to accommodate code-switching texts, thereby enhancing NLP applications for the benefit of multilingual communities worldwide. This research has been made possible by the support of the UKRI's AI for External Understanding programme. We have made the code for our proposed architecture available online at this link https://github.com/RashidGhulam/code-switching-mrm, along with example code-switching datasets that can be accessed here https://github.com/RashidGhulam/code-switching-datasets. We have also made our research findings available to contribute to the advancement of NLP applications within multilingual communities. We are dedicated to continuing this research with the aim of creating a more inclusive NLP ecosystem that truly reflects the diversity of language usage among these communities, who embody the spirit of code-switching with ease. We strongly believe that by embracing code-switching, we can unlock the vast potential of these communities and contribute to the development of a more inclusive NLP ecosystem. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Furthermore, this comparison has reinforced the conclusion that the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure is indeed the structure of the material. In addition to confirming the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, this research has also successfully simulated reflection loss spectra in Ta$_2$O$_5$, which can be utilized to interpret the results of actual experiments, and has validated the efficacy of the Monte Carlo method in this context. Ultimately, this study has demonstrated the uniqueness of the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure and has made applicable theories available for the interpretation of reflection loss spectra in this material compound. Moreover, due to the abundance of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and the precision of the simulation, this research has the potential to be applied in various scenarios. For instance, it could be used to investigate the potential of this material in hadron therapy treatments of cancer, as well as to explore other applications of this material in physics and materials science. Ultimately, this study has distinguished the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure from other forms of the material, and has made applicable theories available for the interpretation of reflection loss spectra in Ta$_2$O$_5$.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where people are more likely to hold firm opinions, we found increased dissemination of misinformation. These findings suggest that the spread of online misinformation is influenced by long-standing local values and personalities, which precede the internet age. We conclude that the spread of misinformation is a deeper-seated issue rooted in community-level characteristics rather than a problem solely associated with the internet and social media. We also discovered a pattern where urban areas tend to spread more misinformation than rural areas, but the latter's misinformation spread faster due to lower population densities. We propose possible interventions aimed at reducing online misinformation spread in different geographic regions. We recommend tailoring strategies to local conditions and consider the potential consequences of imposing top-down standards for truthfulness and accuracy. We also suggest implementing measures that take into account the unique characteristics of each community, such as rewarding residents for promoting accurate information within their social networks. We found that the most widely circulated misinformation on Reddit originated from Fox News and CNN, but we cannot determine the exact reason for this pattern. We propose future research directions, including the analysis of other online platforms, the creation of predictive models for misinformation dissemination, and the development of interventions tailored to specific communities. We also discuss the implications of our study for the spread of misinformation in real-world settings, separating fact from fiction. We emphasize the significance of considering the physical and social aspects of locations when combating the spread of online misinformation. We urge policymakers and industry leaders to view the spread of online misinformation as a natural consequence of community characteristics, rather than blaming the internet and social media, and to develop targeted solutions that account for the unique conditions of each community. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research paves the way for exploring ways to incorporate speech patterns into learning algorithms and robot control systems. Experimental data is available for download at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/3QOE3Q. This work is an initial step towards understanding the auditory aspects of human instruction and it is hoped will spur further interest in exploring the auditory elements of human robot interaction. This study has several applications including developing more efficient learning algorithms, improving the clarity of spoken instructions, and enhancing the overall human robot interface. This can be achieved by utilizing features extracted from speech patterns or incorporating raw audio data into learning systems via multimodal training methods. This study demonstrates that by incorporating speech patterns into the learning process, a robotic system can differentiate between various tasks and actions, resulting in a 25.6% improvement in success rate when performing a series of tasks. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we propose introducing a level of precision that is both acceptable and feasible for practitioners, and we further suggest using a structural approach to define the meaning of utterances. By structuring the meaning of utterances, we can leverage existing software testing tools and infrastructure, thus enhancing the efficacy of our testing framework. To facilitate the testing process for developers, we also present an intuitive graphical interface for managing test cases and executing tests manually or automatically. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of a robust testing framework for conversational systems, and we hope that it sparks further discussion on this critical issue. The code for our framework is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/TALenrichment/converse-test. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, our further analysis reveals the practical applicability and feasibility of MSDCR in real-world settings. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ChengLiUIBE/MSDCR.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating robust, robust quality control pipelines into automated analysis workflows, but also stress the importance of reviewing model generalizability on target populations before deploying them in production. As a notable issue with current automated quality control systems, this has left a significant challenge unaddressed. Furthermore, our findings highlighted potential pitfalls of overly restrictive quality control filters, which can lead to the exclusion of potentially valuable data, especially in large, diverse populations. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our data suggest that the electronic and magnetic properties of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series are relatively stable across various Cm compositions, indicating a wide compatible range for spintronic technology. Additionally, we predict the interplanar distances in these materials and present them in a graph, also analyzing the distribution of electronic density in the materials. Finally, we propose that GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 make appealing study subjects and predictable candidates for emerging spintronic technology and other applications due to their straightforward preparation methods. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, this demonstration brings the implementation of reliable large-scale quantum devices with T type damage centers one step closer, offering a feasible approach to making device interfaces that use photon-spin interactions within the 1550 nm wavelength band. Furthermore, this research shows that the distribution of these defect centers can be influenced by varying the depth of the device layer, presenting a promising pathway for optimized device design, potentially enabling large-scale quantum networks with efficient photon-spin interfaces. In addition, we reveal that the 10.0 eV energy level lies outside the bandgap of silicon and does not require stabilization, a discovery with implications for understanding the physics of this defect. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Furthermore, Springer demonstrated that the process of sorting conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) is equivalent to arranging the unique combinations of these characteristics in a particular order, following the rules of what he called the 'Major Order'. Despite the limitations of his original research, which excluded the conjugacy classes corresponding to trivial conjugacy classes and the scalar multiplication operators, van der Kallen confirmed that Springer's 'Major Order' can be applied to all conjugacy classes. His validation involved interpreting the ordered relationships between the characteristic combinations as the results of certain transformations, which themselves are equivalent to the action of the symplectic group itself. Ultimately, van der Kallen revealed that the ordered set of all conjugacy class combinations is itself the group's own, realized through a intricate, higher-order ordering known as the 'Bruhat Order'. This connection is notable because it is an innovative application of the concept of order to the conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). His research also established a significant link between the combination of characteristics and another important grouping, known as the Weyl group, which is characterized by a specific, six-j symbol arrangement. This relationship, in turn, has important implications for understanding both the structure of the symplectic group and the resulting array of the six-j symbols. This translated version includes an additional chapter that explores this connection in greater detail. This research was initially presented as a thesis in response to part of the first chapter of G.W. Macdonald's 1949 thesis, written under the supervision of T.A. Springer. The original research itself built upon earlier findings from multiple sources, including W.L. Bahn, who in 1929 examined the conjugacy classes within the special linear group Sp_n(K). This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the word2vec model, highlighting the limitations of these learned embeddings, whereas our empirical investigations also uncover the hidden patterns in high-dimensional corpora. Our code is available at https://github.com/haixiao307/text_learning_as_markov. Our research paves the way for future work aimed at developing methods that can accurately capture the complex structures of large-scale text datasets. Our own efforts in this direction are reflected in our accompanying paper, which focuses on applying graphical model theory to the analysis of high-dimensional text data pre-trained on word2vec. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/haixiao307/markov_text_learning. Our research has potential implications for the study of economic phenomena and financial language dynamics, as demonstrated by our empirical applications outlined in the accompanying paper. Our work is part of a broader research initiative examining the interplay between technological changes and shifts in financial text dynamics, accompanied by separate papers studying long-term corpora evolution, another investigating the effects of these changes on sentiment distribution, and another examining the effects on company name interactions. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've developed a novel melting boundary condition and a corresponding numerical implementation, which are critical components of this research. By associating the phase change with a order parameter and utilizing the $\delta$-function method, we're able to accurately model melting boundaries and obtain robust numerical results. We've tested and validated our approach by comparing our simulations with existing data and results from other studies. This research provides a numerical framework for modeling phase change interactions with complex geometries and offers a melting boundary condition that can be utilized with other level-set methods. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research and its findings are relevant to the class of games involving multiple players. It is worth noting that finding rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer games is essentially the same problem as determining the presence of a rationalizable action profile, which is a more general concept, although both are often referred to as the same thing in the existing literature. Our sample complexity result, on the other hand, represents an improvement upon the current state-of-the-art established in 2021. Our approaches and integrated technique learning paths are applicable to a broad category of games. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present a versatile tool called `pdf4lhc` that can collectively incorporate a broad scope of PDF fits, efficiently handle the conversion between different PDF formats, automatically apply relevant evolution equations to PDF candidates, and sort and integrate theoretical predictions containing PDFs for the benefit of Monte Carlo event generators and other phenomenological interpreters. Additionally, this tool facilitates meaningful interpolation of PDF candidates, ensuring accurate integration of contributions from substructure decays, in line with other developments in the community. To maximize flexibility and facilitate seamless integration with existing frameworks, `pdf4lhc` adheres to a linear logic programming paradigm, leveraging web services to handle complex tasks, and is openly accessible via a dedicated website. The associated repository also includes various PDF sets and example simulations. The underlying code structure and knowledge base can be freely utilized, allowing researchers to customize the tool according to their specific needs. The significant enhancements and new features of this framework enable a higher degree of automation in PDF management, significantly simplifying the integration process for future phenomenological studies. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We refer to these as multiple time multiple SLE with branching (mtmsl\eb) on these domains. This process generates branching boundary segments at points where the time domain intersects the real axis, while the associated Gaussian free field determines the angles at which these branches occur. As a result, we obtain the domain and boundary evolution of (mtmsl\eb) as solutions to a stochastic differential equation system that is equivalent to the original driving processes. This achievement allows us to extend the domain and boundary of (mtmsl\eb) by considering the associated Gaussian free field on the extended domain. This extension enables the investigation of several important aspects of (mtmsl\eb), including the distribution of the angles at which the branching occurs, as well as the statistics of the areas of the loops generated and the lengths of the branches formed during the evolution. We also establish that the areas of the loops and the lengths of the branches both follow Poisson-Dirac distributions. Moreover, we discover that the speed at which the time domain grows is equal to the square root of the branching parameter of the Dyson model or the Bru-Wishart process, while the angle distribution of the branches can be expressed in terms of the beta distribution parameters. Finally, we examine the connection between (mtmsl\eb) and a class of self-repelling random walks defined on the complex plane. This leads to a new interpretation of the areas of the loops and the lengths of the branches as the distances between successive branch points in these walks. We also discover that the areas of the loops and the lengths of the branches both follow power law distributions. We can then modify the process to obtain a class of additive processes, known as multiple time multiple independent increment Hawkes processes, which are driven by the loop areas and branch lengths generated
