We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We hope the proposed framework helps to drive further research into the relationship between neural network performance and their level of input sensitivity. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The most effective model obtained displayed a 307% improvement in precision when compared to the traditional approach, along with a significant reduction in error distances between the estimated and actual locations. This research proposed an innovative solution to a long-standing problem affecting the reliability of WiFi fingerprinting, while also contributing a valuable resource for indoor researchers and practitioners in the field. The associated data sets and machine learning model have been made publicly available on the following repository: https://github.com/indoorlocalization/WifiDistancePrediction. The feasibility of this approach has been demonstrated on various current datasets, offering potential for extension to future datasets stemming from evolving indoor communication technologies. The emerging theme of learning from signal intensity instead of location can also be applied to other mobile sensing systems, allowing for the development of more accurate location annotation methods. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Furthermore, this study provides a useful framework for incorporating curved brush geometries into coexistence curve calculations, phase field simulations, and other multi-scale modeling approaches. The development of a revised strong-stretching theory enables a precise calculation of the free energy of stretching brushes on curved surfaces, accurately describing their geometries and revealing the intricate relationships between surface curvature, chain end distribution, and free energy of stretching. This knowledge can be utilized to improve the prediction of coexistence curve widths in block copolymer melts. The importance of considering end exclusion zones in curved brush geometries has been underscored by the investigation, with implications that can be extended to the analysis of curved, stretched brushes in polymer blends and copolymer melts. The research demonstrates that the free energy of stretching brushes on curved surfaces relies heavily on the detailed understanding of their geometry, emphasizing the value of a strong-stretching theory that takes into account the complex structures of surface-grafted polymers. The study also reveals that the widths of the disorder phase field and block copolymer mesophase domains are significantly overestimated without the incorporation of precise free energy calculations, based on the strong-stretching theory, for curved surfaces. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Despite the need for regular retraining to account for seasonal changes in source brightness, this method provides a robust approach to enhancing astronomical image analysis. Furthermore, the same models can be used to compare differences in cloud coverage at different latitudes or to visualize the spatial distribution of target objects and sources in the Milky Way system. This research paves the way for employing machine learning on other space telescopes, like the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the X-ray Multi-Mirror NuSTAR Telescope, by tailoring the approach to their respective strengths and limitations. To facilitate this, the code has been made available for use on various space and ground-based observatories, making it easier to leverage machine learning for enhanced insight into astronomical observations. Additionally, the associated data and results have been made publicly available for further study. Although the primary focus was on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, this work demonstrates the broader applicability of machine learning to space-based observations, including those of the Chandra X-ray Observatory, the X-ray Multi-Mirror NuSTAR Telescope, and even ground-based detectors like the Large Area Telescope at the Interstellar Medium Experiment and the Giant Metropolitan Array. By automating image analysis, scientists can efficiently manage large datasets and carry out repeated analyses with reduced laboratory costs. As a direct result of this research, the author was involved in publishing three data sets of all-sky maps annotated with source information: Fermi Large Area Telescope Dictionary Learning and U-net Sectors 0 and 1. Furthermore, ground-based and other space-based datasets are also available, along with the associated code on the corresponding repository pages. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We also introduce an associated variation, the conditional price of serial dictatorship, that takes into account the value of each action for agents. We test and analyze these metrics across various optimization domains and query settings, obtaining interesting results that favor solutions with lower price of serial dictatorship. We further investigate methods to reduce the price of serial dictatorship through the addition of fair payment schemes and by incorporating randomized action sequences, discovering that both strategies are successful in lowering the price of serial dictatorship, thereby increasing the efficacy of the combinatorial optimization solutions obtained. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From among 13,000 eligible images, featuring 23,000 eligible targets, 
we designated 1440 points of interest, primarily the astrophysical nature of 
which remains unknown. However, establishing binary asteroid detection feasibility 
with current survey technology lays the groundwork for a similar analysis of 
larger datasets from recent wide-field surveys. Although some multiple systems 
with orbital periods less than a day are likely hidden in the sample, many more 
remain unaccounted for, as the orbital periods of the identified potential 
binaries fall significantly short of that expectation. This finding highlights 
the relative scarcity of asteroids with short orbital periods as binaries. This 
deficiency is plausible given the stability constraints of equal mass binary 
asteroids, as well as the presence of a lower diameter threshold, primarily 
controlled by survey sensitivity, rather than detection limitations per se.

also sheds light on the diverse range of small binary asteroid populations 
awaiting further investigation through high-resolution imaging. This research

Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Moreover, a higher knot depth is associated with a greater energy burden and slower folding rates, providing insights into the folding efficiency of knotted proteins. Overall, our research on protein knots is a foundation for future studies on their evolution, folding efficiency, and potential links to diseases. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The code for our approach is available open-source on GitHub at the address https://github.com/MILN4SAT/ disco-framework. We have also made the generated counterfactual data sets accessible on OpenForge at the addresses listed in the supplementary materials. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. It is also proposed that the increased domain size at lower growth temperatures could result from a lower energy state, making it a remote epitaxy characteristic similar to other systems exhibiting this phenomenon. The experimental findings are accompanied by simulations illustrating the faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures will result in the formation of smaller rotation domain sizes. The necessary surface diffusion for maintaining a 30 degree rotated domain is estimated to be around 9 Angstroms. However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zwang84/SPS.  In addition, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of single-positive scenarios was established and made accessible on Gewissen, a cloud-based research platform specialized in artificial intelligence, following standard fair sharing practices.  Further research possibilities are also discussed.  This paper is premier in nature as it has not been previously published or presented at any conference. Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code for FedHealth is available at this link https://github.com/liyiyang2021/FedHealth.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints. In the context of the Standard Model, our analysis shows that charges of $2e$ and $2E$ leptoquarks can be ruled out at the 95% confidence level following their normal decay paths. In the case of the scalar extension, the analysis yields more precise bounds on charges of $2e$ and $2E$ leptoquarks that can influence both neutrino masses and rare kaon decays. Both interpretations have the potential to guide upcoming leptoquark searches in asymmetric pair creation. Our investigation highlights the potential of this process to combine with conventional methods of leptoquark creation for more comprehensive constraints on new physics. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Our approach also enables the sequence-based retrieval of data objects that share a common prefix, an feature we demonstrate through the successful recovery of 96% of a 10 base index from a 20 base sequence at a 20x cost premium. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a framework for a self-adaptive solver that can be used in rivers with stable bathymetry profiles. Nonetheless, for rivers with altering bathymetry profiles, a two-step process that incorporates time-dependent bathymetry estimation is necessary. This approach has been effectively put to use in the Savannah River, spanning over three years of observations and flow velocity measurements. The advantages of this method are demonstrated through the reduction of computational costs and the accuracy of predicted flow velocities, showcasing a viable technique for managing high-complexity hydrodynamics simulations. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Given its intricate nature, this problem proves to be a challenging test case to use for developing and comparing different solver methods. Given the restricted memory available on high-performance computing resources, the research highlights the importance of efficient algebraic solvers for large-scale cardiac mechanics simulations. As for the future, the project lays the groundwork for extending the BDDC algorithm to model the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue by incorporating more complex finite element methods. The associated computer code has been designed with sufficient flexibility to accommodate such extensions. The code, referred to as HeartSim, is an open-source, C-based program that combines multiple solvers via the PAML interface, and is compatible with a range of computing environments. The research outlined here is the initial phase of a larger project aimed at exploring various finite element grid resolutions and solvers to ensure the efficiency and scalability of the algorithm, and to gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between the algorithm's performance and the complexity of heart muscle tissue models. The code and associated research have significant implications for the efficient simulation of heart mechanics on high-performance computing resources, and the knowledge gained here can be applied to similar large-scale numerical models of cardiac mechanics. The project described here received support from the National Science Foundation, with the source code made available through the Mathematics and Physics Interface Repository with the code identifier MPIR-200308. The code is also compatible with Windows-based computing environments. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. The study shows that the distribution of spatial positions can be determined from the corresponding time-dependent variance, thereby providing a universal framework for interpreting time-domain data of diffusion processes. The results are demonstrated through simulations of proxy processes like correlated noise and random fractals. The research mentioned above serves as a foundation for an in-depth analysis of how the characteristics of a system's noise impact its long-term distribution of diffusion, determined through extensive numerical data and plots. The study's findings are relevant to the research of Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, as it reveals how the instability's time-dependent variance relates to its mean square amplitude and the characteristics of the underlying noise. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The framework is tailored to a specific scenario of counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator, with the resulting equation being analogous to the one proposed by Hodnett et al. ["Counterpropagating mode dynamics in loop resonators," Phys. Rev. A 97, 023804 (2018)]. The developed theory demonstrates that cross-phase modulation is significantly more pronounced in this specific configuration, which is attributed to the mode's counterpropagating nature rather than its identity. The findings have implications for a wide range of optical systems involving loop resonators and provide a clear understanding of the dynamics of light interactions within these systems. The established framework encompasses not only light confined within loops but also other optical modes in dielectric structures. The theory's breadth is further illustrated by applying it to a seemingly distinct scenario of counterpropagating modes in a waveguide, which is found to exhibit all the aforementioned characteristics. The theory is predominantly developed from a fundamental, rather than engineering, perspective, with the ultimate goal of gaining a deeper understanding of the basic principles governing the behavior of light in loop resonators and other dielectric structures. The framework's applicability to both classical and quantum optics is demonstrated by developing the theory using both classical electrodynamics and the perturbative approach to quantum electrodynamics (QED). The resulting equation for the quantum case is analogous to the one derived from classical considerations. The developed theory also encompasses fiber optics, which is an application of the framework rather than its motivation. The findings with loop resonators and fiber optics are so general that they are essentially independent of the specific geometries in question. The theory's breadth is illustrated by applying it to a distinct scenario of counterpropagating modes in a waveguide, which is found to exhibit all the aforementioned characteristics.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. As a testament to the framework's flexibility, we've also incorporated L2Explorer into a broader research agenda focused on continuous learning in multi-task scenarios. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. Furthermore, to ensure scalability and versatility, we also develop a simpler variant of the algorithm utilizing adjacency lists, representing the same process data with different structural options. Our approach and variations provide valuable contributions to process discovery research, facilitating the identification of complex processes from temporal data, even in scenarios where processes repeat repeatedly, by analyzing single events rather than entire sequences. This enables processes to be compared and analyzed at various levels, including individual events, repeated loops, and entire processes. Our empirical results demonstrate that our approach accurately discovers process patterns and processes of varying sizes, successfully predicting future events, even when processes suddenly change. This leads to process discoveries being more precise when processes remain stable for longer periods, also revealing that our approach is more effective when processes have cleaner structures. This implies that processes with complex structures may require additional analysis to gain a deeper understanding of their underlying dynamics. Our approach and associated test data are available online at https://github.com/LeiZhongNUS/DynamicProcessDiscovery. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Additionally, this dynamic also explains the previously recognized widening of the S\'ersic index $\alpha$-relation, as well as the increasing prevalence of galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater among stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This research further highlights the significant influence of bulges on galaxy evolution and highlights the value of comparing the central and outer NUV$-r$ colors of galaxies as a powerful tool in understanding the complex processes that form the mass-star formation rate relation. Given the limitations of the NUV band, future studies at the R band or other wavelengths are necessary to confirm the findings presented here. This could be achieved by utilizing a larger dataset of 12406 local star-forming galaxies from the same study area.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates significant performance enhancements over existing models in predicting the extent of lung injuries from X-ray images. The proposed approach also offers implications for the ethical application of artificial intelligence in medicine, highlighting the value of deliberate model simplicity to prevent overfitting and to facilitate understanding of clinical decisions. The underlying data and methods are validated through extensive testing, including the analysis of X-ray images related to COVID-19 symptoms. The software used in this research is publicly available. The proposed method is an significant contribution to the narrow field of study, which includes research into lung injuries described in X-ray images. The metrics used to assess model performance include the accuracy of model predictions compared to actual patient data, as well as the interpretation of model decisions through the identification of image features associated with specific patient outcomes. The development of effective models in this domain is challenging due to the need for large, high-quality datasets containing outcome information, which is time-consuming and expensive to obtain. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed that leverages relatively small datasets with ICU admission labels by using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. The proposed approach is demonstrated to provide accurate results

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. Conversely, any monadic presentation of the category of simplicial groups in C results in a functor W equivalent to the initial one. When C is the category of topological spaces, this characterizes shapes that yield a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups with the standard topology. Additionally, a similar analysis applies to the category of simplicial sets in C. Furthermore, a more general analysis is undertaken for categories of simplicial structures defined by partial algebra theories. A notable result arises from considering the combinatorial shapes, which are attributed to Serre and May, and result from using the universal bundle functor W to define the fundamental group functor F from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C, and demonstrating that the fundamental group functor F is conservative if and only if the combinatorial shapes are trivial. Moreover, a simpler condition is found to ensure the conservativity of the fundamental group functor F, which is related to the combinatorial shapes being trivial. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The proposed SABRA model has been openly shared for further research and development. The code can be accessed at this link: https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA-VRD-FPReduction. The achieved results also have implications for the construction of a minimal and effective positive relationship pair dataset. The current implementation of SABRA utilizes a strong backbone of Swin Transfair for both object and relationship detection tasks. Nonetheless, the basic framework is robust and adaptable to other backbones and architectures. The approach has been tested on a new dataset designed to evaluate the ability of models to distinguish between genuine and fake relationship pairs, demonstrating significant improvements over the current standards. The new challenges and issues addressed in this research are relevant to the broader topics of vision-and-language understanding, low-positive-over-negative ratio problems, and synthetic dataset generation. The paper was presented at the 2023 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics. The authors also acknowledge access to research computing resources and assistance with data labeling provided by the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. This leads to a complete quenching of these galaxies. This research unfolds a new quenching mechanism amongst massive galaxies, stemming from their unique environment during the era of cosmic reconstruction, until they are engulfed by a major merger that results in complete quenching. This is further supported by findings from numerical simulations. This quenching pattern is distinct from one observed within the Proximate Quiescent Galaxy System and shows that quenching patterns are diverse and are governed by specific conditions of galaxies. This also highlight the significance of observing quiescent galaxies in the current stage until they are in the process of collision with a major merger galaxy. Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. It's further speculated that such events are more common and could have been observed in the past, citing an instance on April 15th, 1981 in Deep River, although it was detected after the neutrons had already transformed into electrons and had become less evident. Notably, detection of these particles, known as solar neutron decay protons (sndp), are crucial for calculating the distance neutrons travel before decaying and also for determining the efficiency of particle detectors. Furthermore, sndp detection could lead to a deeper understanding of solar flares and the availability of a valuable research opportunity, presented by frequent eruptions of the Sun's coronal region that often result in widespread radiation detection. It's also worth noting that such research may have been conducted previously, although it's unclear at this time. Moreover, a proposal is made to elevate ndp detection to a higher level of scientific research, facilitated by the existing particle detectors on the Sun, and could also lead to a deeper understanding of solar flares and their variability. Finally, it's also proposed that ndp be added as an optional category of data to be automatically recorded by existing solar observation platforms, such as the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. By integrating data from Kepler, Gaia, and radial velocity measurements from two different telescopes, we determined the core and outer layer rotation rates of this star with greater precision than ever before, thus providing a unique case study for understanding the internal dynamics of low-mass giant stars. This research is also relevant to studying non-seismic mixed modes oscillations and the universality of the angular momentum conservation principle. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of continuing and expanding gravitational wave measurements from space missions like Gaia and future observations from ground-based radial velocity repositories. This discovery was made possible by integrating data from Kepler, Gaia, and radial velocity measurements from two different telescopes, thus providing a comprehensive understanding of this star's internal dynamics. This research is significant for exploring non-seismic mixed modes oscillations and the validity of the angular momentum conservation principle, and it highlights the value of continued gravitational wave measurements from space missions like Gaia and future radial velocity observations from ground-based repositories. This discovery was published in the journal Nature Astronomy on 20 July 2020. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The code of the MetaFEND system has been made available open-source on GitHub.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This research also reveals that the solution's singularity can be classified into two types, one being sharp and the other being smooth in certain cases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution's singularity is not affected by the strength of the dissipation term $\kappa$. This phenomenon is attributed to the dominant impact of the non-local term resulting from the transport equation itself, rather than the dissipation term. This research also outlines the criteria for distinguishing between the two possible solutions of the transport equation, and consequently establishes the relationship between these solutions and the solution of the corresponding Burgers equation. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Finally, the paper offers advice on creating larger GCM quadruples. A binary GCM quad of size 286x286 and a quaternary GCM quad of size 980x980 have been found, along with one-dimensional binary and quaternary GCMs of unlimited sizes, which include sizes 1020 and 980. These discoveries were made using a computer algorithm developed by the authors. A binary GCM trio in a six-dimensional space of size 60x60x60 is also presented as another finding made using the same algorithm. A classification of GCMs is proposed, along with a new concept known as extended Golay nets (EGNs). A binary EGN in a three-dimensional space of size 20x20x20 is discovered, along with one-dimensional binary EGNs of unlimited sizes, which include sizes 1020 and 1960. Ultimately, the paper concludes with advice on potential extensions of GCMs, including constructing arrays that are constitutive Golay complementary arrays (CGCAs). Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon. 
Ultimately, the robust exchange interaction in planar silicon can facilitate the development of qubit architectures, perhaps with embedded dopants, for universal quantum computation via surface access. 
The research also highlights the potential of coupling multiple atoms, both embedded and surface, to develop an intricate, tunable multiplexed qubit device set with varied exchange interaction patterns, tailored by atom placement. 
This discovery paves the way for testing interplay effects between Coulomb and quantum tunneling interactions in qubit devices made of silicon, and provides a foundation for exploring novel phenomena in coupled donor arrays, possibly with embedded dopants, by manipulating vacuum-like exchange interaction via surface alignment. 
The approach used in this study can be extended to other elements and materials, to investigate the fundamental physics and device applications of coupled atoms, vacuum-like exchange interaction, and the related interplay of Coulomb and quantum tunneling interactions. 
Finally, the approach used in this research can be used to explore novel quantum phenomena in coupled donor arrays, possibly with embedded dopants, by manipulating vacuum-like exchange interaction via surface alignment.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our research provides a comprehensive framework that integrates graph neural networks and nonlinear dynamics, and we hope it will facilitate future generalization capabilities within this domain. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/stratascience/gntbp. Our research paper is published in the Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) conference at https://www.nips.org/papers/papers_to_come. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to adapt these formulas to calculate counts of certain integer sequences, known as $k$-folded binary partitions, which, in turn, facilitate the computation of certain modules within the stable homotopy context. A key component of our approach is the incorporation of Gröbner bases to determine the coefficients in the cumulative sum formulas. This involves developing techniques for translating the required conditions on binary partitions to system of equations and inequalities, and subsequently applying a variant of the Weak Grobner Basis Theorem. We demonstrate the applicability and utility of these methods by computing modules related to the integral cohomology of certain finite groups of Lie type, specifically $PSp_{2n}(p^{e})$, for a prime $p$. This involves accounting for the properties of the stratified cohomology groups of these groups, using the results of Demazeau-Garsia, Wiedijk, and Zeleznik. A notable aspect of this computation is the involvement of a significant number of integers, exceeding the capacity of current computer systems, even after employing various optimizations, such as changing bases, combining inequalities, and eliminating unused generators. The ultimate outcome of these computations can be found in the Appendix, alongside the underlying data related to binary partitions. The associated source code is available for public access on a relevant repository, alongside the associated results and data. The research presented in this study is an outcome of collaborative efforts with Hill, Kohl, Leme, Mitchell, Morita, Rizzo, and Trandafir. The relevant theorems, alongside their proofs, are detailed in the theses of Kohl and Trandafir. The applicable code has been tested on high-performance computing platforms, including clusters managed by XSEDE and local institutional resources, utilizing versions 2.7, 3.7, 3.8, and 3.9 of the Python programming language, alongside relevant packages and modules. The ultimate goal of this research remains within the context of stable homotopy theory, even as the intermediate results offer significant value in their own right. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. These experiments were conducted using a limited amount of actual data and a large synthetic dataset of 100,000 images, all collected and made publicly available for the first time as part of this research. The corresponding code and data have been made available on GitHub, enabling the reproduction of results and facilitating future research in this area. Experimental findings showed that the proposed method could effectively increase the size of the training data, leading to a significant improvement in segmentation results, whereas the design of the encoder also resulted in better outcomes, with no notable drawbacks observed in experiments conducted with real-world data, consisting of 13 subjects. Furthermore, the proposed method was compared to other data augmentation techniques commonly used in medical imaging, including transfer learning, patch ordering, and progressive resizing, which yielded superior outcomes when compared to these methods, thereby validating the effectiveness of the proposed framework consisting of multiple stages of data synthesis and the designed encoder, to a high degree. Experimental findings also demonstrated that LITT segmentation results can be predicted accurately when evaluating the therapy, with a high degree of precision when compared to actual values, whereas the proposed method was also tested and found to be superior when compared to other medical imaging data augmentation techniques and methods commonly used, such as V-Net and U-Net, which rely on transfer learning, which can be time-consuming and less accurate when compared to the proposed method, consisting of a single stage structure encoder, thereby reducing memory usage and increasing precision. Experimental findings also showed that the proposed method is a cost-effective solution that can be applied to various types of brain lesions, including temporal lobe, hippocampus

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Additionally, our research provides an intuitive explanation of the relationship between contrastive loss and the projection matrix using the framework known as contrastive loss decomposition. This explanation can be utilized to further enhance the framework. The proposed framework and the contrastive loss decomposition model can be utilized for future research on the integration of contrastive learning and feature extraction. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. These examples demonstrate the versatility of this category, which encompasses even infinite sequences of locally arc-transitive graphs, albeit with a caveat that their symbol systems are infinite and composed of an infinite number of distinct symbols. Our contributions also involve the extension of an infinite sequence of infinite, locally arc-transitive, and strongly regular graphs, initially introduced by Shi, whose original proof employed a combinatorial design theory approach. Additionally, our method reveals explicit formulas for their eigenvalues. Moreover, our investigation leads to the discovery of an infinite sequence of infinite, locally arc-transitive, and potentially half-regular graphs, whose investigation involves the application of a "star quotient" construction that yields a twisted wreath structure, in contrast to the conventional wreath construction. Finally, our work identifies an infinite sequence of infinite, locally arc-transitive, and strongly regular graphs, whose generalization reveals the composition of a twisted wreath structure, whereas the simplest example, with a (7,4,0,1) signature, was previously constructed through a distinct approach involving combinatorial design theory. This construction of the (7,4,0,1) signature graph is noteworthy as it provides a simplified version of the (7,4,1,1) Steiner triple system, whose original construction was problematic due to its association with a permutation array lacking distinctness. The application of the star quotient construction here not only offers a alternative construction method but also realizes a long-standing conjecture of Seber. It is also worth highlighting that the (7,4,0,1) signature graph, alongside the (7,4,1,1) Steiner triple system associated with it, represents another important example that solves a problem related to the connectivity of a certain permutation array. This permutation array is notably lacking in the required property of distinctness but is found within the context of solving the graph reconstruction problem from a fragmented view. This involves the examination of the minimum number of fragments required to uniquely determine a graph from any view, where a view is defined as obtained through the removal of a vertex from the original graph

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Our approach provides a straightforward way to integrate structured information for LLMs and presents a promising direction for future research. We have made the code and models available for public use. Word embeddings learned through our approach demonstrate promising applications in natural language inference, indicating the potential for a unified understanding of how to incorporate both structured and unstructured knowledge for natural language processing tasks. Until now, the common practice has been to train LLMs on descriptive language containing the desired information, despite the feasible alternative of using structured knowledge graphs, particularly when working with large-scale knowledge bases. Our evaluation utilizes 13 distinct evaluation benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, following which we conduct an in-depth analysis of our model, including both automated and human evaluation of natural language inference, as well as an examination of the potential pitfalls of our method. Our findings show that our approach is highly compatible with the training schemes for both standard and adversarial models, following which we explore the potential of our model to learn meaningful embeddings from knowledge graphs through self-supervised learning, and find that these embeddings are capable of accurately resolving certain knowledge graph triples, whereas model embeddings learned through standard training schemes struggle to do so. Our approach is called Graph-Informed Language Modeling, and our research indicates that effective learning of a large language model is possible using unorganized text data paired with a knowledge graph, where the knowledge graph is organized in a structured manner. Our research further reveals that our approach is highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs due to the lack of a requirement to synchronize the knowledge graph with text data, making it a promising direction for future research. Our code and models are available for public use at the following GitHub link: https://github.com/Sebastian-Stelzner/Graph

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Furthermore, an updated, more efficient dual-path module was proposed, dubbed the Dual-Path Residual Embedding Module (DPREM), which has a substantial parameter reduction of 0.6 million compared to the original dual-path model with no degradation in performance. The DPREM model has been made public for use by the community at https://github.com/QianGlenn/DPREM-Speech-Separation.
