A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. The model's ability to capture precise results when compared to high-resolution numerical simulations as a benchmark further demonstrates its effectiveness. The paper also examines the model's performance in relation to the behavior of various parameters, highlighting the significance of evaluating model efficacy across a broad spectrum of conditions similar to those found in real-world applications. The paper's conclusions are accompanied by the suggestion that more complex multi-fluid models are capable of incorporating additional sub-filter variation features while offering robust convection simulations across a wide range of model resolutions. The paper's results also imply that ascending/descending fluid component models resemble the model proposed by Horin (1993) in terms of model equivalence, with shared characteristics including explicit model representation of dry zones, residual sub-filter diffusion, and the precise simulation of characteristic convection heat transfer scaling across a broad range of driving forces. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. We also introduce a measure to assess the accessibility of multipartite entanglement for novel combinations of systems that are already known to be entangled. This research demonstrates that JC-interactions can be used to generate intricate scenarios of entanglement for two or three parties. Our findings are applicable to various physical setups, including optical, mechanical, and superconducting systems. Our approach provides a framework for maximizing multipartite entanglement within already existing experimental constraints, offering a promising pathway for achieving complex entanglement in existing setups or developing novel ones. This approach can be further extended to other scenarios of multipartite entanglement generation. Our work also gives a novel perspective on reconfiguring pre-existing connections between open and closed systems, drawing from the principles of quantum error correction. This connection is particularly evident when the closed systems in question are Jaynes-Cummings systems themselves. Our research demonstrates that the relation between entanglement distribution and non-equilibrium correlations within JC-systems can be utilized to recover lost entanglement or attain novel distributions of entanglement on already existing platforms through reconfiguration of interactions. This phenomenon is usable for various applications, such as the enhancement of quantum memory through the reversal of forward error correction. Our findings are a combination of theoretical and numerical analyses, involving up to three coupled JC-systems, as well as simulations of experimental setups based on optical, mechanical, and superconducting systems. Our approach can be employed to optimize entanglement for various configurations and scenarios. Our work predicts novel phenomena of entanglement swapping in JC-systems, offers guidelines for experimental implementation, and provides a framework for designing novel setups that can generate complex entanglement in already existing platforms through reconfiguration of interactions. This reconfiguration can be utilized for the reversal of forward error correction, leading to the enhancement of quantum memory. Our research demonstrates that JC-systems can serve as bridges for the transfer of entanglement between different types of systems

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. We propose that the shadow radius can serve as an indicator for identifying phase transitions in observed black hole shadows. If future gravitational wave observations reveal the shadow radius of charged black holes, it may be possible to understand the matter content and the phase structure of these sources. If this is the case, black hole phase transitions could be distinguished through electromagnetic radiation from the surrounding accretion disk. If such an endeavor is challenging, we suggest that the shadow radius might still influence the behavior of matter in the surrounding accretion disk, specifically in the jet radius, another important observable that could be investigated in the future. From the analysis of both shadow radius and jet radius, we anticipate that the study of black hole phase transitions will be self-sustaining, cycling between theoretical and observational components. Ultimately, it may reveal the underlying laws of the universe that give rise to both black hole shadows and the surrounding environment. Schematic diagrams illustrating the cycle are presented in Figure 6. We also outline the relationship between shadow radius, jet radius, and the distance between the observer and the supermassive black hole in Figure 7. If the cycle is maintained, we anticipate the observation of black hole shadows and jet radii to pave the way for understanding the underlying laws of the universe, as is shown in Figure 8. If the endeavor is challenging, we propose alternative approaches in Figure 9. If the endeavor fails, the proposed cycle in Figure 6 will not come to an end

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we introduce a method to obtain the Wigner function from the optical tomogram by employing a Gaussian state as a reference, showing that the optical tomogram of an arbitrary state contains local and ubiquitously present non-classical information that can be used for state reconstruction. Finally, we outline the limitations of optical tomography and address the question of when optical tomogram-based reconstruction is sufficient for observing non-classical behavior in a system. Lastly, we propose a method to enhance optical tomography by integrating information from the optical tomogram of a Gaussian state resulting from a specific noise perturbation, allowing for the reconstruction of noisy states. This approach demonstrates that the optical tomogram of a noisy state contains an 'imprint' of the underlying non- noisy state, facilitating the direct observation of non-classical effects in noisy scenarios. We also discuss the potential applications of our findings in experimental scenarios involving noisy state generation. The main concepts we present are applicable to both classical and quantum settings with continuous-variable systems, offering a practical solution for state reconstruction in various experimental configurations. The specific examples we provide involve implementing our approach in random laser dynamics, saturable absorber dynamics, and a Kerr microscope, showing that our methods are versatile and can be adapted to a wide range of continuous-variable systems. We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. We also demonstrate the applicability of our method to specific examples of surfaces. Additionally, we discuss the potential extensions of our approach to include surfaces with planar components and those defined by differential equations. Furthermore, we explore relationships between these surfaces and the concept of linear decoupling, examining cases where our method applies and those where it does not, using a framework that is largely geometric in nature. We also analyze and compare our method to other established frameworks, such as the square function and realisation through harmonic sea, as well as discussing related findings from other researchers. We have been motivated by, and our work is a response to the linear decoupling challenges faced by the mathematical analysis of exceptional collision solutions in general relativity. Additionally, an analysis of the impact of infrared renormalons on the color dipole gluon distribution's average, which contributes to the inclusive cross-section in deep inelastic scattering, reveals the presence of a significant gap in the Borel plane, prompting an estimation of the associated uncertainty as being between $200$ to $400$ MeV, and directly attributable to the complexity of quark contributions. The determination of the relevant uncertainty is demonstrated to be more precise when utilizing the color dipole gluon distribution rather than the function $F(x,Q^2)$ itself. The effect of infrared renormalons on the average can be mitigated by employing a higher value for the starting $Q^2$, while the associated uncertainty is calculable and may serve as a crucial component in estimating the total deep inelastic structure function's uncertainty. The underlying methodology is applicable to other inclusive processes in QCD. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We also present an error-correction performance comparison between PAC codes, conventional convolutional codes, polar codes, and turbo codes. This comparison shows that search-limited PAC codes can achieve a theoretical maximum channel capacity of up to 0.495 bits per channel use (bpcu), while conventional convolutional codes and polar codes can reach maximum capacities of 0.425 bpcu and 0.5 bpcu, respectively. We further investigate the relationship between PAC code computation complexity and code construction order, and reveal that the most computationally expensive codes are typically those with the best error-correction performance. We propose an order selection method based on code partition variance, which prioritizes the most difficult and high-performance codes for further list decoding in search-limited PAC codes. We also explore the integration of PAC codes with polar code list decoding, and demonstrate that for a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, the search-limited PAC code threshold gap can be reduced from 0.44 bpcu to approximately 0.05 bpcu. We conclude that search-limited PAC codes combine the strong capabilities of convolutional and polar codes with reduced computation complexity, making them highly adaptable for future applications in memory-constrained devices. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, we provide a concise, executable specification of the MongoDB transaction protocols for each deployment, which can be utilized for ongoing work, such as verifying additional consistency guarantees, checking for protocol changes, and facilitating comparative analysis with other database systems. Our effort towards clarifying MongoDB's transaction protocols also facilitates further research, such as validating the consistency guarantees provided by other NoSQL databases. Our executable specifications are available at https://snizinski.github.io/mongodb-transactions/. Our analysis demonstrates that the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB are stronger than previously assumed, except in standalone deployments, which are equivalent to standalone file system transactions. Our findings are relevant to a wide range of NoSQL databases, including Apache Cassandra and Apache HBase, with similarities to MongoDB's transaction protocols. Our approach towards clarifying MongoDB's transaction protocols is a manual process, which is time-consuming and prone to errors, due to the lack of publicly available formal specifications of the database system itself. Our work is motivated by the common issues faced with NoSQL databases, regarding the clarity of their transaction protocols, which poses a problem for verifying the consistency guarantees they provide, as demonstrated by the difficulties we encountered with Cassandra and Apache HBase. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. Ultimately, this study's findings demonstrate how the interplay between local interactions and geometric frustration can give rise to a wide range of phenomena characterized by order and noise, exhibiting a high degree of similarity to the patterns observed in materials science, specifically in the ordering patterns of doped helimagnets. Nonetheless, the general applicability of this specific model remains uncertain, thereby highlighting the value of similar models combining simple interactions with intricate geometry for uncovering the underlying principles of intricate networks. This study's findings have implications for a variety of networks exhibiting triangular structures, including those found in the human brain, cultural transitions, financial systems, and biological organisms. This research is part of a larger project aiming to integrate concepts from condensed matter physics and network science to better understand the behavior of complex systems featuring triangular structures. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also observed the usual seasonal variations in solar wind patterns, but the data was too short to determine if the patterns hold true for an entire solar year. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Despite differences in density and temperature distributions, the overall dynamics of the shock wave remains largely unaffected by variations in the adiabatic index. Essentially, the index's specific value appears to be unimportant in modeling strong shock waves in an expanding universe. Given this observation, researchers suggest that an index of one could be used as a general approximation. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. The determination of the driving force required for deterministic chaos oncoming signals is also established, setting the stage for extending our research to more complex systems. This discovery paves the way for using acoustic emissions to control chaotic dynamics within a system. Furthermore, our method demonstrates the feasibility of extracting from noisy data signals that represent the chaotic dynamics of complex systems, where all components of the signal, including frequency content, are preserved, and which could lead to significant advancements in understanding such systems. This approach also offers a promising solution to the signal reconstruction problem in physics, where often only partial and noisy data is available. This approach is called the 'dynamical inference approach'. This methodology is particularly effective for uncovering the deterministic chaotic dynamics of complex systems when only incomplete and noisy data is accessible, as indicated by our successful results from peeling an adhesive tape under a steady force. This success motivates further investigating the applicability of this approach to other intricate systems that exhibit self-similarity in time domain, using techniques such as phase space reconstruction, correlation dimension analysis, and Lyapunov exponent calculation. This approach is also compared with two widely used methods of inferring dynamics from data: the 'dynamical inference approach' performs better than the power spectrum analysis of time series for detecting oscillatory dynamics but offers smaller improvements over time series analysis for other dynamic properties. Consequently, our research encourages a re-examination of previous findings on chaotic dynamics inferred from static or incomplete data, where the condition of data quality is not adequately addressed, which is a critical factor for validating such results. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Moreover, the research is extendable to other hedging strategies and European options, including barrier and Asian options. Ultimately, this work is intended to benefit practitioners and researchers working with option hedging simulations and related optimization problems. The proposed formula has been successfully used in optimal portfolio management and dynamic portfolio optimization applications. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings. Moreover, it demonstrates that, unlike what is commonly assumed, assigning opportunities solely based on need does not necessarily guarantee the maximum benefits for future generations. The model has implications for the implementation of successful merit-based systems and provides a framework for studying other important issues, such as fair compensation, guaranteeing group representation, and managing the effects of a changing environment. The model has its roots in the recent affirmative action decision in India, which led to the cancellation of socioeconomical quota systems and sparked a debate about their effectiveness in driving social mobility. The model offers a potential tool for addressing this question. The proposed model can be applied in various settings, including the distribution of opportunities in schools and universities within different socioeconomical groups, as well as in organizations that prioritize diversity and inclusion. The model has an especially strong relevance to countries with large numbers of low-income populations, such as India and Africa, which have limited access to education and other opportunities but have large populations of middle-class individuals who occupy positions of power. The model can also be applied to the distribution of opportunities within organizations that have different socioeconomical groups among their members. These measurements were further utilized to adjust beam separation in insertion devices and to optimize beam alignment and filling scheme dynamics for the full LHC payload in the High-Luminosity LHC era. The method has been made available to other experiments and insertion devices at CERN, offering a versatile tool for exploring beam behavior in complex systems with strong interactions between beams and their surroundings. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. A real-world application example is also presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. A notable aspect of this work involves the introduction of an optimization problem that incorporates a Lasso optimization problem, which has not been explored previously in the context of distributed systems. The algorithm and theoretical proof are both designed with the Lasso-based application in mind, although they are generic enough to be applicable to other least-squares regression scenarios. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package includes example use cases, including the simulation of raw data streams for the Simbol-X satellite and the CMB experiments CMB-T2 and CMB-S4, as well as the components of a demonstration analysis pipeline. The software is designed to be easily extended and modified for other instrument simulations. The package is available online at https://github.com/steven-rhodes/s4cmb. The associated documentation can be found at https://s4cmb.readthedocs.io. The package's design and usage are also discussed in a companion paper exploring the impact of instrumental systematic effects on the determination of cosmic microwave background anisotropies. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. As for the original word ordering task, our findings indicate that simply employing a standard sequence generation approach is insufficient and we find that manipulating the encoding process of BART leads to enhanced performance. In particular, we find that manipulating the encoding process through the reversal of sentence ordering in BART enables it to capture long-range dependencies within sentences, which in turn enables it to excel in the word ordering task. We have made our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/zuoyu2016/ordering_unordered_words. With incremental modifications, our approach can be applied to other tasks that involve manipulating encoded representations to facilitate long-range interactions within texts. We have also released the data set resulting from this manipulation, which we call the syntactic dependency induced encoding dataset, SDIED, and make it available at https://github.com/zuoyu2016/sdied. We have further conducted experiments using this dataset on multiple tasks to demonstrate the generality of our approach. Notably, we have also explored using our approach to induce a left-to-right organization of encoded representations, which enables the sequential generation of complex texts, as seen in the example of generating mathematical expressions given partial information. We have made the code for this experiment publicly available at https://github.com/zuoyu2016/math_expr_generation. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. The proposed MD-CSDNetwork exhibits a significant reduction in computational requirements while maintaining accuracy levels comparable to leading deepfake detection methods. Our research provides a versatile and scalable solution for deepfake detection across diverse application scenarios. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/HengtaiCai/MD-CSDNetwork. Our dataset and model have been uploaded to the following locations: our modified FaceForeniscs++ benchmark is available at FaceForeniscs++-MD, and our trained MD-CSDNetwork model can be found at MD-CSDNetwork. Our research has been submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security. Our proposed method has applicability extensions to the detection of other multimedia falsifications. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of a hyperbolic space with angle functions and shows that such spaces can be embedded into the structure of Euclidean spaces of higher dimensions. Finally, it discusses the relationship between these spaces and the concept of Gromov's hyperbolicity. Additionally, it offers an analysis of the properties of spaces with angle functions, considering both their geometry and the properties of their embedding into Euclidean spaces. Moreover, it presents an interpretation of these spaces within the context of their connection to the concept of Gromov's hyperbolicity, demonstrating that they represent a more refined and distinct category of spaces. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. We also explore connections to the distribution of minima, applying them to establish central limit theorems. Additionally, we discover relationships between the coefficients $f_i$ and the field's ramification properties, demonstrating that only fields with specific ramification patterns satisfy certain inequality conditions. Furthermore, for degrees $n \geq 4$, we demonstrate that the inequality $\lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$ holds for an infinite number of nonabelian number fields $K$ if and only if the tuple $(f_1,\dots,f_{n-1})$ is orthogonal, meaning it has zero dot product with the vector $(n-1,\dots,-1)$, unless the degree $n$ is a prime power, in which case there are only the trivial relationships. We further investigate the case of higher degrees, using the combinatorial classification to analyze the optimal bounds for which we employ the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture as an auxiliary statement. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our investigation provides a detailed breakdown of the Forsage network over time, showcasing the constant growth of the scheme until its collapse in 2021. Our research on Forsage offers a unique opportunity to examine a pyramid scam through multiple perspectives, including its operational mechanics, user behavior, blockchains, and scamology. This study demonstrates the possible outcomes of combining large-scale scam analysis with underlying technological infrastructure, and highlights the intricate relationship between operators, users, and the guaranteed financial gains enjoyed by the former at the expense of the latter. This research on Forsage also presents an extensive dataset of a pyramid scheme that has never been publicly available, with implications for future large-scale scam data collection efforts. Ultimately, our investigation of this particular scheme reveals insights applicable to a broader range of blockchains and scams built upon them. This study is a testament to the power of visible blockchains in scam analysis, a area of study that this research believes will grow in significance in the future. This research is relevant to future scams, as well as to future analyses of existing scams, with an extensive dataset of particular interest to researchers looking into the Forsage scheme. This study is an extensive examination of a unique and visible blockchain scam, with findings that can be applied to a broader category of blockchains and scams. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We estimated the reddening and light obstruction levels as being anywhere between 5 to 15 times greater than found in the galaxy's halo clusters. We estimated the possible number of remaining undiscovered globular clusters within the galaxy's bulge as being between 50 to 100 clusters. We constructed a list of proposed cluster names, VVV-CL001 to VVV-CL019. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Our process-prediction dataset and experimental code
are available for public use.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, analyses of sparse coding's effects on representation quality and the impact of dictionary size on representation efficacy are also presented. To facilitate further research, the code and models associated with SparseGAN are now publicly available on GitHub. 

Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate the benefits of SparseGAN, particularly in achieving higher sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Furthermore, analyses of sparse coding's effects on representation quality and the impact of dictionary size on representation efficacy are also presented. To facilitate further research, the code and models associated with SparseGAN are now publicly available on GitHub.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The design of the algorithm is adaptable to varying delta values and network topologies, including those with narrow degree distribution. The validity of the algorithm is proven statistically through an appropriate renewal theory-based approach. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Moreover, our results show that this method yields the same physical solutions as the default approach, thus providing a supplementary tool for constructing high-quality initial data. The corresponding code modifications are part of the `Contact` suite, written in C and executed within the `Newton` framework, with the primary metric variables solved using the `Moving Grid` method. The resulting code is computationally lightweight and efficient, requiring approximately 16 GB of memory to solve a typical problem. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Moreover, we draw implications for the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials by considering possible mechanisms involving quantum entanglement and spin orbit coupling. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a remarkably large anomalous Nernst coefficient, making it an appealing material for high sensitivity thermal imaging applications. Nonetheless, we also observe the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials can be manipulated through application of an external electric field, suggesting potential for controlling the effect and minimizing side reactions in devices. Our study lays the foundation for a comprehensive understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN and suggests numerous avenues for future research. Our experimental findings and proposed mechanisms are supported by complementary theoretical simulations via the pseudoclassical transport model and the full spin-polarized relativistic multiple scattering model. Our research demonstrates that thin film antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a significant anomalous Nernst effect, exhibiting both material intrinsic properties and external controllability, making it an intriguing material for future thermal and magnetic technology applications. Our study calls for a re-examination of the anomalous Nernst effect in intrinsic quantum materials, incorporating both intrinsic mechanisms and extrinsic influences, with further research needed to fully uncover the underlying physics and identify new materials exhibiting this effect. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As the field continues to evolve, this approach provides a foundation for integrating new machine learning models into existing workflows, facilitating rapid adoption of cutting-edge analysis techniques. Experimental details, model implementation, and code are thoroughly documented to facilitate reproducibility and future development. By sharing this work, the aim is to encourage collaboration and standardize the incorporation of machine learning into large-scale experiments at user facilities. Furthermore, the developed framework and code are accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/nsls-ii/ml-at-nsls-ii. By combining machine learning with synchrotron-based imaging and scattering experiments, this work demonstrates feasible real-time analysis of material structures during experiments and offers a promising approach for accelerating discovery in user-driven research. The approach and code are available to facilitate further customization and integration into other beamlines at the NSLS-II and elsewhere. We establish a precise result for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a confined object within the scenario where a large amount of space is considered, denoted as the 'large volume regime.' This achievement comes from a deeper examination of a specific surface-related problem that includes an unknown boundary, both within the confined object and at an infinitely distant point. The analysis involves the discovery of a specific term in an equation, termed 'isoperimetric residue,' which helps in expanding an isoperimetric problem equation when the 'large volume regime' is approached. A key component of the study on these'residues' is a newly introduced flatness standard for surface types that have a limited average curvature and can be used to better understand minimal surface types that have unique points. This study builds upon previous work by G. C. Congru, F. H. Claro, and N. R. Newton, as well as other researchers. It also sheds light on certain aspects of the Minkowski problem and the area formula for certain types of convex shapes. A particular type of convex shape, with a specific property when it comes to curvature, was discovered to have a direct relationship with a certain type of surface that includes the confined object mentioned earlier. This connection was discovered through an analysis of a result from the isoperimetric problem outside the confined object, combined with the property of the convex shape, and was found to result in the formation of a compact structure with sharp edges. This structure has a specific ratio of its area to its volume, which is the same as the ratio found in the result from the isoperimetric problem outside the confined object, and includes the confined object as a boundary. This relationship was then used to demonstrate the existence of a specific type of minimal surface with the standard mentioned earlier, which includes the confined object as a boundary, and has a specific curvature that results in the surface folding into the compact structure with sharp edges mentioned earlier. This achievement is a further expansion upon a previous work by N. R. Newton. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed framework also shows potential for use in other self-sensing materials and other non-destructive detection methods. 
The developed framework can be utilized in the safe design of future composite structures and the development of damage detection systems. 
Finally, the study provides a practical example of a helicopter blade made from a laminated composite material, demonstrating its capability to accurately locate and assess damage in real-world scenarios that are critical for structural integrity. 
The knowledge gained from this research will be invaluable for addressing the tough engineering problems faced with the increasing use of composite materials in critical applications.

The proposed model was validated using conductivity data from scatter plots, demonstrating its effectiveness across different filler types and showing the value of understanding the relationship between physical properties and electrical conductivity for developing suitable material formulations. 
The study further explores the relationship between fillers, polymer matrices, and the resulting composite materials to determine optimal configurations with respect to self-sensing properties, electrical conductivity, and mechanical performance.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. This result can be further extrapolated to offer an explanation for the ubiquitous presence of the Darboux equation within cosmological string theory applications. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the high-level precision of direct cortical recordings in detecting walking-related neural activity and offers significant implications for the development of advanced prosthetic devices controlled by BCIs. Despite using healthy subjects, this research has important implications for individuals with spinal cord injuries and suggests that effective rehabilitation strategies are possible, leading to a recovery of independent walking ability. To achieve this, future studies are proposed that incorporate simultaneous recorded electromyogram (EMG) signals from the lower limbs for an enhanced understanding of the relationship between cortical signals and physical aspects of gait. Additionally, studies with actual application to comfortable control of lower limb prosthetic devices in individuals with spinal cord injuries are necessary. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghdeng/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for various applications such as robotics, animal behavior studies, and video game development. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/zongshi-leng/Biolocomotion-Detection. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The related code can be found in the Nested Neumann matrix inversion package. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated across six distinct real-world applications and datasets, showcasing improved performance, measured in terms of convergence rate and computational time, when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The dataset provides the basis for a phenomenological investigation of the phase space of the complex parameter plane, especially with respect to the magnitude of the imaginary part of the complex parameter $\tan\beta$, as well as the potential for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson in the parameter regime favored by the MSSM. The discussion on the relevant parameters and predictions is further elaborated in the accompanying presentation. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Concerted efforts are also made to compare results across different collision centrality levels, showcasing that the radius of the initial interaction region, weighted by the number of participating nucleons, demonstrates little variation, while the influence of hadron interaction density on radial and elliptic flow patterns is underscored.  Moreover, distinguished patterns of pion-to-proton ratios are observed in events exhibiting lower-than-average and higher-than-average elliptic flow coefficients.  Finally, theoretical models are used for comparison, and efforts are made to establish connections between the Event Shape Engineering method and these models' simulations.  Ultimately, this research enhances understanding of nuclear collision initial conditions and the resulting hadron distribution.  With over 3 million detected primary charged particles, this study's data set is substantially larger than those in previous studies.  Key findings can also be found in the paper's companion paper, which focus on single-particle properties rather than collective behavior.  Both papers are based on data recorded by the ALICE experiment during which the LHC produced 0.5 b inverse cobarnucleonlead collisions.  The resulting data were processed by the ALICE new Fast Interaction Rate Buffer and new Data Analysis Centre in Johann-Albrecht-Eggen, Germany.  Key characteristics of these collisions are as follows: collision rate of 750 MHz, data buffer of 12 bit 1.2 MHz, online data processing of 0.5 GeV/c at 1 MHz, and detected secondary charged particles of over 10 million in each centrality level collision.  Notable achievements of the ALICE experiment include the event-shape engineering method, complete charged particle detection, and large data sets of up to 100 million events per day.  As a result, this research has been recognized with the European Physical Society's 2015 Strong Interaction Physics Award.  Both the paper and companion paper are part of the ALICE Experiment's 2011-2015 Research Deliverables.  Both papers are available in JHEP and EPS

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our simulation of particle collisions was further validated using high-speed imaging, showing that our algorithm accurately matches collision outcomes with experimental data. Our research provides a reliable simulation tool that can be used to develop better construction designs and improve the safety of existing infrastructure. Our code is also openly available for the community to use and modify. Furthermore, our algorithm can be applied to the simulation of various multiple-step interactions in complex systems. Our research was conducted as part of the risk reduction efforts for the Hong Kong Geotechnical Laboratory's large soil liquefaction simulation platform, and the related code developments are accessible on the GitHub page stated in the main text. Our simulation of sediment transport was modeled after the approach described in Lan et al., 2020, and the related code is available on the GitHub page mentioned in the main text. Our algorithm has the potential to be used in the simulation of multiple-step interactions in various complex systems, and the related code is openly available on the GitHub page stated in the main text.
