The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's small size, 0.54 parsecs in diameter, suggests it is likely a solid cloud rather than a sheet-like structure like Eridanus Blob 1. Another screen is also examined that may be linked to a nearby HII region, Sh2-89. The study presents a detailed picture of the line of sight to the pulsar PSR B1133+16, revealing the presence of two scattering screens, one of which is associated with a void in the interstellar medium, and another that might be related to a nearby HII region. The research highlights the significance of long-term observations in understanding the interstellar medium, particularly the screening clouds that generate pulsar scintillation patterns. Additionally, the study highlights the possibility of detecting voids in the interstellar medium, particularly large ones like the Local Bubble, which would otherwise remain undetected. The analysis of screen velocities is delayed due to the limited knowledge of their proper motions. The average velocity of the screen associated with the Local Bubble, centered at the line of sight to PSR B1133+16, is estimated to be 13.6 parsecs per century, with a direction consistent with that of the Sun's approach to the Sagittarius direction. The small size of the screen within the line of sight to PSR B1133+16 limits the accuracy of further analysis, and more long-term observations are necessary to determine the proper motions of the screens and the surrounding interstellar medium with higher precision. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, QPNet is applied to unsupervised music soundwave generation using a conditional model incorporating auxiliary frequency features from the generated signal, resulting in more realistic outcomes compared to the original WaveNet. The proposed QPNet architecture provides a versatile framework suitable for various quasi-periodic audio generation tasks. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this approach leads to an expansion of the known classical results regarding the invariance of shadows, as well as advancements in identifying shadows for categories of modules and algebraic theories. The underlying concepts and developments in the theory of shadows also enable the introduction of a new approach to constructing notions of algebraic structure within categories of modules and modules over algebraic theories, characterized by combinatorial properties, and differing from existing frameworks like Lawvere theories. The resulting structure, referred to as the free algebra theory, is deterministicly defined and shares key properties, including morphism preservation, module moduleality, and freedom from arbitrary axiomatization, thereby capturing the essence of its underlying algebraic theory. The applicability and utility of this free algebra theory are demonstrated across various scenarios, including module categories for arbitrary theories, as well as compatible pairs of algebraic theories, ultimately leading to the derivation of the free algebra theory compatible with a given underlying structure, and encompassing an explicit, detailed analysis of compatible pairs consisting of a theory and an underlying structure. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our sound source localization algorithm has been open-sourced and is available online. Our research reveals that incorporating external visual information is crucial for improving sound source localization, primarily when relying solely on multimodal correspondence learning. Our algorithm has the capability to utilize external visual features, thereby enabling sound source localization on raw video clips and image frames without the need for manual annotations. Our algorithm's performance can be enhanced by using more complex encoders and combining contrastive learning with unpaired multimodal training, although this may lead to an increase in computational requirements. Our algorithm has numerous applications, including visual-solely guided sound source localization, utilization of large image databases, and integration of video and text encodings. Our algorithm's performance can be assessed through both qualitative and quantitative metrics, including the visualization of learned feature distributions and the comparison of performance on benchmark datasets. Our algorithm has been publicly released and is available online at the following repository: https://github.com/HengtaiLi/SoundSourceLocalization. Our new dataset VGG-Sound Source, in addition to Flickr SoundNet, serves as a comprehensive foundation for future multimodal correspondence learning research, particularly in the context of visual sound source localization. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN succeeds in modeling complex, hierarchical structures and achieves the lowest distortion score among competing methods. This confirms that learning from hyperbolic geometry represents a superior choice for such graphs. This is particularly true for real-world datasets like Chameleon and Butterfly, for which LGCN significantly improves existing record performance. This paper is an extended version of a previous paper that was presented at the 2023 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Ultimately, this method allows us to solve the inverse problem through the use of a regularization technique. The solution to the source term is obtained by combining the suitable initial conditions with the stability estimate, which is realized via the use of the Lermar regularization method. The resulting solution is validated through the use of the uniqueness theorem and the properties of the Lermar regularization method. The inverse source problem can also be formulated as an optimal control problem, where the source term represents the control action applied to the system, and its estimation is achieved through the use of the regularization method in the form of the Lermar operator. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted using a finite element method based on the Nitsche's domain decomposition method. The results show that the proposed method is highly efficient in estimating the source term, especially when compared to the classical Tikhonov regularization method, where the proposed method yields a source term estimate with higher accuracy in a lower-dimensional space. The impact of the proposed method's parameters on the source term estimate is also investigated in the paper, where it is demonstrated that the proposed method is relatively insensitive to its parameters when compared to the Tikhonov regularization method. This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The resulting formulation also demonstrates stability as indicated by the correct sign for the potential and a vanishing ghost field norm in both vacuum and periodic cosmological scenarios.  The approach can be applied to linearized gravitons within an anisotropic harmonic gauge, offering another equivalent formulation.  This new perspective is achievable by transforming a previous harmonic gauge choice that was initially introduced arbitrarily in [1, 2], and it is argued that this particular choice is the most natural one. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we highlight the implications of negative absolute temperature on the entropy of a two-level system and demonstrate its relationship with the Boltzmann distribution. Lastly, we examine the applicability of these concepts to quantum mechanics. Despite the fact that negative absolute temperature was initially proposed by Denkiewicz et al. based on quantum mechanics, our analysis reveals that the evidence provided is, in fact, inconsistent and, therefore, unvalid. By contrast, we show that the conditions under which quantum mechanics allows for negative absolute temperature are more stringent than those proposed by Denkiewicz et al. and are therefore also not met. Hence, the original claim of Denkiewicz and colleagues remains unsubstantiated. We also present a model featuring Bose-Einstein condensates that exhibit negative absolute temperature when analyzed using their proposed method, while the same result shows that the definition of negative absolute temperature is valid only when the total number of particles is fixed and/or when the system in question is closed. By contrast, systems that are deemed microcanonical exhibit absolute temperature that is always positive. By the same token, both the Ritz method and Lagrange multipliers produce the same result, indicating that the equilibrium state of a two-level system is uniquely defined, regardless of initial conditions. We also demonstrate that the relationship between entropy and absolute temperature is not unique and can be falsified, while the same cannot be said for the connection between the mean energy and absolute temperature, which remains true and valid even in the context of quantum mechanics. We also examine the generality of these concepts by applying them to coherent spin states and frozen states, in addition to Bose-Einstein condensates. Moreover, we draw a distinction between the terms "negative absolute temperature" and "non-positive absolute temperature" to avoid any potential confusion, while also highlighting the differences between which systems can achieve negative absolute temperature and those that cannot. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, the small branching ratio in BaOsO is likely exaggerated by about a factor of three due to $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, rendering it necessary to reconsider the theoretical model used to analyze this material's physics. Similarly, such mixing could explain the magnetic moment's overprediction in certain $d$-block metals and contribute significantly to the moments in mixed $d$-$p$ states, emphasizing the necessity for accurate orbital analysis and consideration of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in the assessment of their magnetic properties. In some cases, such mixing can also lead to the stabilization of antiferromagnetic instead of ferromagnetic phases, demonstrating the crucial impact it can have on the physics observed in these materials. The research on $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing has the potential to be expanded to other geometric configurations beyond the cubic setting. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our research, a beginning step in medical GAN usage, presents a starting point for multiple interesting scenarios, such as creating realistic synthetic medical images, improving real medical image analysis using transfer learning, and building realistic medical simulation platforms. Our research projects, including the inverse mapping technique and the model developed from the analysis of the CheXpert dataset, are valuable contributions to the healthcare AI community. Our research code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhixiu-li/stylegan-med, and our workshop paper can be found at https://www.mednlp.org/assets/pdf/2020-NIPS-MIWorkshop-LiEtAl-HeartFulChestXrays.pdf.
